audiences: Readers interested in neuroscience, behavioural causation, free will, moral luck, punishment, and inequality
People willing to separate the strong causal science from the disputed philosophical conclusion
Policy and justice readers considering how explanation should alter blame without abandoning safety or behaviour change

sources.title: Determined: The Science of Life Without Free Will — sample
sources.supports: UK edition facts, full contents, author statement of purpose, positions opposed, causal framework, style, and previous works.
sources.limitations: Fifty-three-page sample containing front matter and the opening chapter, not the complete book.

sources.title: Determined
sources.supports: US publication facts, argument, author position, biological and social examples, justice implications, clarity, and breadth.
sources.limitations: Concise favourable trade review without a detailed philosophical audit.

sources.title: Determined: A Science of Life Without Free Will
sources.author_or_publisher: John Martin Fischer; Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews
sources.supports: Whole-book structure, US metadata, scientific breadth, definition problem, compatibilist counterargument, responsibility critique, and cited passages.
sources.limitations: A strongly critical assessment by a leading compatibilist; its philosophical objections are relevant but contested.

sources.title: How Can Determinists Believe in Free Will?
sources.supports: Implications for blame and praise, distinction between Sapolsky's test and ordinary concepts, moral-practice objections, and delivery.
sources.limitations: Philosophical review essay rather than a line-by-line check of the biology.

sources.title: Determined: Life Without Free Will — the hard science of decisions
sources.supports: Causal-chain strategy, implications, scientific density, humour, voice, and reservations about the book's philosophical move.
sources.limitations: General-audience review rather than specialist verification of every scientific field.

sources.title: A Critical Review of Determined: Life Without Free Will
sources.supports: Clinical and neuroethical criticism of the move from no free will to no culpability, incarceration as quarantine, and predicted humanitarian effects.
sources.limitations: Single-author journal review; challenges Sapolsky's ethics more than the causal neuroscience.

sources.title: Turtles All the Way Up
sources.author_or_publisher: Jessica Riskin; The New York Review of Books
sources.supports: Historian-of-science criticism that the no-free-will conclusion exceeds what science can establish and depends on a mechanistic philosophical commitment.
sources.limitations: Strongly critical and partly paywalled; interpretation is disputed directly by Sapolsky.

sources.title: Half-Cups Runneth Over
sources.author_or_publisher: Robert Sapolsky, reply by Jessica Riskin; The New York Review of Books
sources.supports: Sapolsky's direct defence that no single discipline settles the issue but their interlocking causal knowledge collectively leaves no free will.
sources.limitations: Author's reply defending the book, followed by the reviewer's disagreement.

sources.title: The Free Will–Determinism Debate in Contemporary Science and Society
sources.author_or_publisher: Frontiers in Human Neuroscience via PubMed Central
sources.supports: Current comparison of Sapolsky's deterministic position with Kevin Mitchell's agency account and discussion of chaos, emergence, quantum physics, and social consequences.
sources.limitations: Broad debate review rather than an experimental adjudication of free will.

sources.title: Determined
sources.supports: Large reader aggregate and recurring praise for breadth, humour, and compassion alongside criticism of length, repetition, determinist overreach, and uneven philosophy.
sources.limitations: Self-selected ratings and reviews, edition merging, and no control for expertise or completion.

sources.title: What's Wrong With Determinism? Review of Determined
sources.supports: A naturalist sympathetic to Sapolsky's rejection of contra-causal freedom who clarifies change, control, practical responsibility, and the distinction between determinism and fatalism.
sources.limitations: Advocacy organisation committed to philosophical naturalism and broadly aligned with the book's anti-libertarian position.

workflow.coverage_notes: The publisher's complete contents and opening chapter were checked directly, then every later chapter and major argument was triangulated through philosophy, neuroethics, science, legal, professional, author-response, and reader sources. No uninterrupted lawful full text was available.
next_steps: Optional: verify every endnote and extended case against an owner-supplied or library copy to promote coverage to full-book.
